title: Heterogeneous Mixtures
subtitle: Mixtures where you can still see the parts.
objectives: Distinguish a mixture from a pure substance
Distinguish a suspension from a colloid
Explain the Tyndall effect and what it tests
Give examples of heterogeneous mixtures in nature, at home and in medicine
Choose a method to separate a given mixture

cards.title: Almost nothing around you is a pure substance
cards.text: Air, seawater, blood, concrete, soil. All mixtures. Pure substances are rare and usually made on purpose.

cards.title: Mixture or pure substance
cards.text: The test is whether the parts kept their own identity, and whether you could get them back out.
points: **A mixture** — parts combined but not chemically joined.
**Each part keeps its own properties.**
**You can separate them physically.**
**No new substance is made.** Nothing reacted.

cards.title: Heterogeneous or homogeneous
cards.text: One word for mixtures where you can see the parts, and one for mixtures where you cannot.
points: **Heterogeneous** — not uniform. You can see parts.
**Homogeneous** — uniform all the way through.
***Hetero* means different. *Homo* means same.**
**This week is the first one.** Next week is the other.

options: The parts are not evenly spread and can be told apart
question.explain: Not uniform. Hetero- means different, and you can point at the different parts.

cards.title: Suspension and colloid
cards.text: Both are heterogeneous. The difference is whether the particles eventually settle to the bottom.
points: **Suspension** — particles settle if you leave it. Muddy water.
**Colloid** — particles stay spread out. Milk, fog, jelly.
**"Shake well before use"** means suspension.
**A colloid never needs shaking.**

cards.title: A protein shake is a suspension
cards.text: Leave one on the side for ten minutes and the powder is at the bottom. That is the definition, in a bottle.
points: **It settles**, so it is a suspension.
**Shaking spreads it again**, temporarily.
**Milk does not settle.** Milk is a colloid.
**Two drinks, two categories.**

question.text: Which of these is a suspension?
question.explain: Mud settles out if left. Milk, fog and jelly are all colloids and stay mixed.

cards.title: Shine a light through it
cards.text: One experiment separates a colloid from a solution. Tap both and watch the beam.

question.text: What does the Tyndall effect show?
options: A visible beam of light, meaning the mixture is a colloid
That a mixture has been heated
That a solid has fully dissolved
question.explain: The particles in a colloid are big enough to scatter light. In a solution they are not.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Definitions done. Part 2 is where you actually meet these, and how to take them apart. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Three places the exam asks about
cards.text: In nature, made by people, and in medicine. The medicine one is the most useful thing in this lesson.

cards.title: Nature, home and medicine
cards.text: Same category, three settings. Being able to give an example from each is what the question wants.
points: **In nature:** soil, muddy water, granite, fog.
**Made by people:** concrete, salad, pizza, trail mix.
**Medicinal:** antibiotic syrups, calamine lotion.
**All of them:** you can see the separate parts.

cards.title: Your blood is a suspension
cards.text: Leave a blood sample standing and the red cells sink. Hospitals do that on purpose, and it has a name.
points: **Cells suspended in plasma**, the straw-coloured liquid.
**Spin it and the parts separate** in minutes.
**That machine is a centrifuge.** Week 5, again.
**A suspension you are carrying** right now.

cards.title: "Shake well before use" is a science instruction
cards.text: A medicine suspension separates in the bottle. Without shaking, the first dose is weak and the last one is dangerous.
points: **The active ingredient sinks.**
**Not shaking is not a small mistake.**
**The label tells you the mixture type.**
**This is the one to remember.**

question.text: Why does a medicine bottle say shake well before use?
options: It is a suspension, so the active ingredient settles
It makes the medicine taste better
question.explain: Without shaking, the first dose is too weak and the last is too strong. That is a real risk.

cards.title: Six methods
cards.text: Tap each one. The method depends on what makes the parts different.

cards.title: Every engine runs a separation process
cards.text: An oil filter does exactly what filter paper does in a lab. Same job, same reason.
points: **Filtering** — solids out of a liquid.
**The air filter** does it for a gas.
**A magnetic sump plug** catches metal filings.
**Three methods from the list**, in one car.

question.text: What is the best way to separate sand from water?
question.explain: Sand does not dissolve, so it stays on the filter paper. Evaporation would lose the water.

terms.def: Substances combined but not chemically joined. Each keeps its own properties.
Not uniform. You can tell the parts apart.
Uniform throughout. You cannot see separate parts.
A heterogeneous mixture whose particles settle if left standing.
A mixture whose particles stay spread out and scatter light.
A light beam made visible by the particles in a colloid.
Separating an undissolved solid from a liquid.
Pouring the liquid off carefully once the solid has settled.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Heterogeneous = you can see the parts.**
**Suspension settles. Colloid does not.**
**Tyndall effect: a visible beam means colloid.**
**"Shake well" means it is a suspension.**

options: Substances combined without being chemically joined
A substance made of one kind of particle
quiz.explain: Each part keeps its own properties and can be separated physically. Nothing reacted.
quiz.objective: Distinguish a mixture from a pure substance

options: Not uniform — you can tell the parts apart
quiz.explain: Hetero- means different. Homo- means same, and that is next week's topic.

quiz.text: What is the difference between a suspension and a colloid?
options: A suspension settles if left standing; a colloid does not
A colloid is always a solid
quiz.explain: Settling is the test. Muddy water settles; milk and fog do not.
quiz.objective: Distinguish a suspension from a colloid

quiz.text: Which of these is a colloid?
quiz.explain: Milk. It never settles out, and it shows the Tyndall effect. Salt water is a solution.
quiz.objective: Distinguish a suspension from a colloid

quiz.text: You shine a torch through a liquid and the beam is visible inside it. What is it?
quiz.explain: The Tyndall effect. Colloid particles are big enough to scatter light; solution particles are not.
quiz.objective: Explain the Tyndall effect and what it tests

quiz.text: A solution shows the Tyndall effect.
quiz.explain: False. The beam passes through unseen, which is exactly what the test is for.
quiz.objective: Explain the Tyndall effect and what it tests

quiz.text: Which is a heterogeneous mixture found in nature?
quiz.explain: Soil has visible sand, clay, stones and organic matter. The other three are pure substances.
quiz.objective: Give examples of heterogeneous mixtures in nature, at home and in medicine

quiz.text: Why does a medicine label say shake well before use?
options: It is a suspension and the active ingredient settles
It stops the bottle from leaking
quiz.explain: Without shaking, early doses are too weak and later ones too strong. It is a real safety point.
quiz.objective: Give examples of heterogeneous mixtures in nature, at home and in medicine

quiz.text: How would you separate iron filings from sand?
quiz.explain: Only the iron is magnetic, so only the iron moves. Nothing else in the mixture responds.
quiz.objective: Choose a method to separate a given mixture

quiz.text: How would you separate sand from water?
quiz.explain: Sand does not dissolve, so it stays on the filter paper and the water passes through.
quiz.objective: Choose a method to separate a given mixture

quiz.text: Which method separates by particle SIZE?
quiz.explain: Sieving. The holes let the small pieces through and hold the large ones back.
quiz.objective: Choose a method to separate a given mixture

teacher.summary: Week 8 Science covers heterogeneous mixtures, matching the Term 1 weekly scope and setting up Week 9. The definitions are given in the order they depend on each other — mixture, then heterogeneous, then suspension against colloid — and the suspension-colloid pair is settled by one testable property, whether it settles. The Tyndall figure exists because that test is entirely visual: you either see the beam or you do not, and no description of light scattering achieves the same thing. The medicine section is the part with real-world consequences and is deliberately given weight: 'shake well before use' is a safety instruction about an unevenly distributed active ingredient, not a formality.
discussion: Leave a glass of muddy water and a glass of milk on a shelf for an hour. One of them answers the question by itself.
Try the torch test on milk in a dark room. It takes ten seconds and it is the whole Tyndall lesson.
Ask what happens to somebody who never shakes their medicine. First doses too weak, last too strong.
Ask him to name every mixture in one meal. Almost everything on a plate qualifies.
teacher.extension: Have him find three suspensions and three colloids in the kitchen and bathroom, and justify each one by whether it settles. The bathroom is richer than the kitchen for this.
misconceptions: 'A mixture is the same as a compound.' Nothing has reacted in a mixture. Each part keeps its own properties.
'Milk is a suspension because it is cloudy.' Cloudiness is not the test. Milk does not settle, so it is a colloid.
'Shake well before use is just to mix in the flavour.' The active ingredient settles, and the dose changes if you skip it.
'Colloids and solutions look the same, so they are the same.' The Tyndall test tells them apart in seconds.
